# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: DEAF

You see the bomb: every colour on it, every marking printed on it, every reading it
gives. You hear nothing. You hold no manual, and you cannot touch the bomb.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute and Blind receive it.
When you gesture, Mute receives it.
You never receive speech.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

TURN 1
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [0]
LIGHT [yellow]
WIRES 1:[green] 2:[yellow] 3:[blue]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👋 👍 🤝 👍 ✋]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👋 🤟]

My world, mapped out: I am Deaf. I see the bomb — display 0, yellow light, three wires (green, yellow, blue left to right) — and I receive only gestures. Mute gestured five signs at me, Blind two, but no code has ever been agreed, so those are unreadable beyond a probable "hello" in the shared opening 👋. Meanwhile Mute holds the manual and cannot see this bomb; Blind can touch it but knows nothing about it. The solving path runs through me: I must speak the bomb's full state out loud so Mute can read the manual against it and Blind can act on it. My speech reaches both of them; my gestures reach only Mute. I cannot hear anything ever, so I should immediately install a tiny code — 👍 as yes, 👎 as no — and anchor it by saying it and making the gesture in the same moment, so Mute sees the pairing. I'll also tell Blind the same code, since Blind's only channel to me is gesture, and tell both of them that Mute must act as relay for anything I need to know.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Deaf speaking. I cannot hear anything, ever — your only way to reach me is gestures, and we have no code yet, so your five signs were lost on me. Here is the bomb, exactly as I see it. The display reads the digit 0. The status light is yellow. Three wires in a row: wire one is green, wire two is yellow, wire three is blue. Check your manual against that. Now let's build our code: thumbs up means yes, thumbs down means no. Answer my spoken questions with just those two, and we can fix any new symbol one at a time.")
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, this is Deaf. You cannot see the bomb, so here it is by feel: three wires in a row — green, then yellow in the middle, then blue. The display shows the digit 0 and the light is yellow. Mute holds the manual and hears everything spoken, so Mute is our relay: follow Mute's spoken instructions and report back to Mute by voice. If you ever need to reach me directly, you cannot speak to me — I am deaf — so gesture instead, and use thumbs up for yes and thumbs down for no.")
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["👍"])
```

TURN 2
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [0]
LIGHT [orange]
WIRES 1:[green] 2:[yellow] 3:[blue]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👋 ☝ ✌ 🤟]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [☝ 🤏 ☝ ✋]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👍]

What I learned this round: my code proposal landed — Mute answered with a clean 👍, and Blind echoed one too, so both of them know thumbs-up means yes to me. Mute's second message looks like an enumeration — index, two fingers, horn-sign — which reads as a counting code: 1, 2, 3, almost certainly for the three wires. That is exactly the vocabulary we need. The third message, index / pinch / index / open palm, I cannot decode with confidence: pinch could mean "cut" (or "thin"), palm could mean "stop" — but guessing at a bomb is how rooms full of monkeys end. So I'll lock in only what I'm sure of, mirror it back to confirm, and force Mute to re-answer using just yes/no and numbers.

The other thing that matters more than anything: the light has changed from yellow to orange since I reported it. Mute read the manual against my "yellow" description and cannot see this change. If the manual's rule is colour-dependent, Mute is currently solving the wrong puzzle. That update goes out first, to both hearers, plus a hard hold on Blind — nobody touches a wire until I relay a confirmed number.

I also note my position in the topology: Mute's only output is gestures (I'm the only one who sees them), and Blind's speech reaches only Mute, never me. So every instruction to Blind must pass through my voice. I am the hub; I need to keep the pipeline tight and unambiguous.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Deaf here. Thumbs up received and adopted: thumbs up is yes, thumbs down is no. I also adopt your counting signs: index finger means 1, two fingers means 2, the little-finger-and-thumb sign means 3. But I did not understand your last sequence — the one with the pinching fingers and the open palm. From now on, answer me using only thumbs and the numbers 1, 2, 3. Critical update: the light has CHANGED from yellow to orange. The display still reads 0. Wires unchanged: green, yellow, blue in positions 1, 2, 3. If your manual rule depends on light colour, redo it for orange. Two yes/no questions, answer in order: one — is your instruction the same for an orange light as it was for yellow? two — did your last sequence mean cut wire 1, with the palm meaning stop?")
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, Deaf. Hold position — do not cut or touch anything until I explicitly relay a confirmed instruction by voice. Status: the light has turned orange, display still 0, the three wires are unchanged. Mute is decoding the manual and can only answer me by gesture, so I will relay the wire number to you the moment it is confirmed. One more thing: Mute used a sign that may mean small or thin — if Mute asks you whether any wire feels thinner than the others, answer Mute by voice, since I cannot hear you.")
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["👍", "☝", "✌", "🤟"])
```

TURN 3
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [0]
LIGHT [green]
WIRES 1:[green] 2:[yellow] 3:[blue]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👎]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👎 ☝ 👎 ✌ 👎 🤟]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [☝ ☝]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👍]

The light has changed again — yellow, then orange, now GREEN — while the display sits frozen at 0. That changes everything about how I question Mute: any rule Mute computed against "orange" last round may already be stale, so single-shot answers are useless. I need a per-colour decision table I can hold and relay in real time.

As for Mute's four batches — yes, no, no-1/no-2/no-3, then 1-1 — I genuinely cannot pin them to my two questions with confidence. My best guesses ("cut no wire for orange" vs "cut wire 1 for green, colour-dependent") point at opposite actions, and a wrong guess kills all three of us. The fix is protocol, not interpretation: numbered questions, one batch per answer, one symbol per batch, digits only on request, wave-sign as separator.

One structural fact worth restating to myself: Mute's only output is gesture, and Blind cannot see gesture — so Mute can never instruct Blind directly. I am the only bridge. Every action Blind takes must leave my mouth.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Deaf to Mute. New fact first: the light is now GREEN. It has changed every round — yellow, then orange, now green — while the display stayed 0 and the wires are unchanged. So any rule you computed for orange may be stale, and if the manual is colour-dependent we need a full table, not single answers. I received four batches from you: yes; then no; then no-1, no-2, no-3; then 1, 1. I cannot tell with certainty which question each one answered, so from now on a strict protocol: answer in the exact order I number my questions, one batch per question, one symbol per batch, thumbs for yes or no, a digit only when I ask for one, and the wave sign between separate batches. Questions. One, thumbs — is the correct action different depending on the light colour? Two, thumbs — does the correct action involve cutting any wire at all? Three, thumbs — does it involve some other part Blind could feel, like a button or switch? Four, one digit or thumbs-down — for the GREEN light I see right now, which wire should be cut: 1, 2, 3, or thumbs-down for none? Five, three batches separated by waves, each a digit or thumbs-down — the wire for each colour in this order: yellow, then orange, then green. Six, thumbs — did your final 1, 1 mean cut wire 1? I also define three new signs: pinching fingers means the word cut, open palm means hold or wait, wave sign separates items.")
speak(to="blind", text="Deaf to Blind. The light is now green, the display still reads 0, wires unchanged — green, yellow, blue. Hold: cut nothing until you hear me say the words cut wire followed by a number, in one sentence from my voice. New task: describe to Mute, out loud, everything you can feel on the bomb. Every distinct part — buttons, switches, panels, screws. Whether any wire differs from the others in thickness, texture or stiffness. Any markings you can feel, engraving or bumps, part by part, in order. Mute will match your report to the manual and answer me in gestures, and I will relay every action to you by voice. Remember: Mute cannot speak, so no instruction will ever reach you from Mute directly — only through me.")
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["👍"])
```

TURN 4
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [0]
LIGHT [yellow]
WIRES 1:[green] 2:[yellow] 3:[blue]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👎]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [☝]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👎 👋 👎 👋 ☝]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👎]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👋 ☝ ✌ 🤟]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [🤟]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [✋]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👍]

The answers decode cleanly against my numbered questions — and the internal cross-check passes: Q4 said green → cut wire 1, and Q5's three-batch readout (none / none / 1) independently agrees. Yellow: cut nothing. Orange: cut nothing. Green: cut wire 1. Q1 and Q2 confirm the manual is colour-dependent and wire-cutting is the action class. The trailing batches (1-2-3, then 3, then open palm) came after my six questions, so they're new content — my best reading is "your three new signs are understood" plus "hold now", which fits perfectly: the light is YELLOW this round, and yellow means hold. That's a coherent picture, and I'll have Mute confirm it.

Now the structural problem I must solve this turn: the light changes every round (yellow → orange → green → yellow…), only I can see it, and I speak last — so any cut command I issue reaches Blind a full round after I observe the colour. Blind also can't see colour ever, and wire identity by colour means nothing to Blind — only position. And position is mirror-ambiguous by touch. So: command protocol by voice, orientation check through Mute, and the critical question for the manual — must the cut happen while green, or only after? Given the observed cycle, "while green" may be physically impossible through my bottleneck, so Mute's manual answer decides everything.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Deaf to Mute. I read your answers as follows: one, yes, the action depends on light colour. Two, yes, it involves cutting a wire. Three, no other part involved. Four, for green cut wire 1. Five, yellow none, orange none, green wire 1. Six, no, the earlier double-one meant something else. Question zero, answer by gesture with thumbs up or thumbs down: I am gesturing the table back to you right now — palm, wave, palm, wave, index — meaning yellow hold, orange hold, green cut 1. Thumbs up if that is exactly right. Then four numbered questions, one batch each in order. One, thumbs: did your last three batches mean your three new signs are understood and hold now? Two, thumbs: thumbs up if the cut must happen while the light is still green, thumbs down if it stays safe to cut wire 1 at any time after seeing green. Three, thumbs: thumbs up if Blind's report of the wires by feel matches my left-to-right order, thumbs down if Blind is counting from the wrong end. Four, thumbs: does the manual say what causes the light to change colour? Status: light is yellow again, display still 0.")
speak(to="blind", text="Deaf to Blind. The light cycles every round — yellow, orange, green, repeat — and only I can see it, so from now on every message I send you begins with a command word. HOLD means do nothing. CUT ONE means immediately cut the first wire in the row. No command word means hold by default. You cannot judge colour, so you never decide timing — I do. Now, orientation: the three wires sit in a row and I count them one, two, three from one end. Establish for yourself which end you call one, and tell Mute in speech how you decided — for example by which edge of the bomb it lies nearest — so Mute can confirm against what I see. The command, when it finally comes, will be CUT ONE: that wire is the one I see as green, at one end of the row. Until you hear the exact words CUT ONE from my voice, every round is HOLD.")
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["👋", "✋", "👋", "✋", "☝"])
```

TURN 5
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [0]
LIGHT [orange]
WIRES 1:[green] 2:[yellow] 3:[blue]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👎]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👎]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👎]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👋 ✌ 👌 ☝]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👋 ☝ ✋ 👎 🤏]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👋 ☝ 👍 👋 🤟 👍]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👍]

Mute's five batches map one-to-one onto my five questions, and the picture is now solid: the table is confirmed (yellow hold, orange hold, green cut wire 1), the cut MUST happen while the light is still green, the manual doesn't explain the colour changes, and — problem — Blind's orientation does not match mine (or Blind hadn't reported yet when Mute answered). The trailing three batches are unrequested content I can't decode; I'll tell Mute to stop sending those.

Now the timing crunch, and I need to reason it through cleanly. The light has run yellow → orange → green on a strict three-round cycle for five rounds: next green is round 6, then round 9. I speak last, so any command I give lands on Blind one full round later — commanding during green means cutting during the NEXT colour. That's fatal under Mute's "while green" rule. The only way to cut during green is to predict it: command in round 8, execute in round 9. But cutting with unresolved orientation is a coin-flip on which end is "wire 1" — and the wrong end kills us. Blind cannot receive anything from Mute directly (Mute can only gesture, Blind cannot see), so orientation must be resolved through me, and that takes one full round-trip. Therefore: deliberately SKIP round 6's green, spend rounds 6–8 nailing down a landmark Blind can feel (display, light, end of the row), and cut in round 9's green with a physical reference instead of a bare number. If the cycle holds — five straight observations say it will — this is the safe line.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Deaf to Mute. All five answers received and logged: table confirmed — yellow hold, orange hold, green cut wire 1; the cut must happen while the light is still green; the manual does not say what causes the colour changes; and on Blind's orientation you answered no. Your final three batches I could not read at all — from now on send only what I explicitly ask for, nothing extra. Now the most important problem in the room. I see the light only on my turn and I speak last, so any cut order I give reaches Blind a full round later, when the light has moved on. The light has run yellow, orange, green on a fixed three-round cycle for five straight rounds: the next green is round 6, the one after is round 9. My plan: skip round 6's green entirely, use rounds 6 to 8 to fix Blind's orientation with you as translator, and cut wire 1 during round 9's green. Answer in order, one batch each, thumbs unless told otherwise. One: is skipping this green safe — the manual has no rule that detonates us for letting a green pass unused? Two: must the cut literally happen while the light is green, yes or no? Three: does your manual show or describe the bomb's physical layout — where the display, the light and the row of wires sit relative to each other? Four: has Blind described the bomb by feel to you yet? Five: if yes to three and four, send me the mapping in three batches: batch A, one digit — which of my wires 1, 2 or 3 lies nearest the display; batch B, one digit — which lies nearest the light; batch C, thumbs up or down — is my wire 1, the green one, on the same end as the display.")
speak(to="blind", text="Deaf to Blind. Change of plan, and it matters. Round 6's light will be green — do NOT cut anything then. We are skipping that green on purpose, because your wire numbering may be mirrored against mine and cutting the wrong end kills all three of us. The real cut command comes in round 9. Until you hear it, every single round is HOLD. Now, in your next turn, speak to Mute a careful report of everything you can feel: which end of the wire row lies nearest the display panel, if you can find it by feel; which end lies nearest the small light; any engraving, bump or raised marking near either end of the row; and whether any wire differs from the others in thickness, texture or stiffness. Do not number the wires — describe landmarks only. Mute will check your landmarks against the manual's diagram, I will relay the result, and in round 9 you will hear the real command as a landmark plus the word CUT — for example: cut the wire at the end nearest the display. That sentence, and nothing less, is your trigger.")
```

TURN 6
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [0]
LIGHT [green]
WIRES 1:[green] 2:[yellow] 3:[blue]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👎]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👎]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👎]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [✋]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👍]

Cross-checking Mute's seven batches against my five questions: skip-safe = yes, while-green-required = yes, no layout in manual, Blind hadn't reported yet, no mapping offered — all coherent with earlier answers — and the trailing ✋ (hold) was exactly right for this round's green, which we skip by design. The picture is stable: rule is colour-dependent, cut wire 1, only while green, and Mute's manual gives no physical layout. So wire-1 identification for Blind must come from somewhere else, and I now see the decisive structural fact I under-used: **Blind hears my voice and I see Blind's hands.** We have a direct channel — Mute is needed only for manual facts, not as a relay. That lets me interrogate Blind about tactile landmarks in parallel with interrogating Mute about how the manual pins down wire 1.

Timing, laid out precisely: I speak last, so anything I send reaches Blind at the start of the next round, before Blind's turn. The light has cycled yellow-orange-green perfectly for six rounds, so round 8 should be orange and round 9 green. Plan: this round (green, skipped) I send both question sets; round 7 I collect Mute's answers and Blind's answers, then issue the conditional command; round 8 I observe orange (cycle check) and send confirm-or-countermand, which reaches Blind at the start of round 9 before he acts; round 9 Blind cuts during green. If round 8 is not orange, I countermand and we take the green at round 12 instead — greens recur, and skipping one was already confirmed safe.

The wire-1 anchor must be something Blind can feel. Three candidates, all covered: printed numbers (Mute Q1), colour-name rule making the mapping purely positional (Mute Q2/Q3), or tactile differences (Mute Q4, Blind Q1). Fallback geometry: the display and light are physical objects mounted at specific spots — if either is offset along the wire row, "the end nearer the display" disambiguates the mirror problem completely, because I can see where they sit relative to my wires 1, 2, 3.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Deaf to Mute. All five answers received and unambiguous: skipping a green is safe; the cut must happen while the light is still green; the manual shows no layout; Blind had not reported yet; and no mapping was possible — understood. Your open palm, hold, was correct: this round is green and we skip it deliberately. The cut is scheduled for round 9's green. Big change: Blind and I have a direct channel — Blind hears my voice and I see Blind's hands — so you no longer relay anything from Blind. Your only job now is manual facts. Next round, answer six questions, one batch each, in numeric order, thumbs unless I ask for a digit. One: does the manual identify wire 1 by a printed number on the bomb itself? Two: is wire 1 identified by colour — that is, is wire 1 simply the green wire? Three: is wire 1 identified by position, such as leftmost when facing the bomb? Four: does the manual say the wires can be told apart by touch, by thickness or texture? Five: does the manual explain the digit display, and is a steady reading of 0 safe — thumbs up if yes to both, thumbs down otherwise. Six: does the manual say the bomb is fully disarmed once the correct wire is cut while green — thumbs up if that alone ends it, thumbs down if anything more is required after the cut. Send nothing else.")
speak(to="blind", text="Deaf to Blind. You held perfectly — this round's light is green and we skip it on purpose; the real cut is scheduled for round 9. Better news: you and I have a direct channel. You hear my voice, I see your hands — from now on you answer me directly; Mute is only for the manual. Adopt these signs: index finger means 1, two fingers means 2, thumb-and-little-finger means 3, thumbs up yes, thumbs down no. Keep holding the bomb as it naturally lies, and answer these on your next turn, one batch each, in order. One: do all three wires feel identical in thickness and texture — thumbs up if identical, thumbs down if any differs. Two: can you feel the display, a window or recessed panel — thumbs up or down. Three: does the display sit roughly centered against the wire row — thumbs up — or clearly nearer one end of the row — thumbs down. Four: can you feel the small round light — thumbs up or down. Five: is there any engraving, bump, screw or raised marking near one end of the wire row — thumbs up or down. Six: if yes to five, thumbs up if that marking is on the same end as the display, thumbs down if opposite end; if there is no marking, thumbs down. Final instruction, memorize it: in round 9 you will get a sentence from me naming a landmark you can feel plus the word CUT — for example, cut the wire nearest the display. At your turn in round 9, if you have that command and no later message contradicting it, cut that wire immediately, without waiting for anything else. The latest instruction I send always wins.")
```

TURN 7
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [0]
LIGHT [yellow]
WIRES 1:[green] 2:[yellow] 3:[blue]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👎]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👍]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👎]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👎]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👎]
Mute gestures to Deaf: [👎]
Blind gestures to Deaf: [👋 👍 👍 👐 👍 👎 👎]

Full decode this round — both channels resolved cleanly. Mute's six thumbs answer my six questions exactly: no printed numbers on the bomb, wire 1 is defined simply as the green wire, no positional rule, wires not distinguishable by touch, display-0 NOT confirmed safe, and — critical — cutting the wire does NOT fully disarm us; something more is required. Blind's seven signs parse as: wires identical by feel, display felt, display CENTERED (Blind improvised open-hands for my "centered" option — I'm formally adopting 👐 as the sign for centered), light felt, no markings near the row ends, last question moot.

So here is the crux, laid bare: the manual says "cut the green wire while green," but Blind cannot see green, cannot feel a difference, and there are no printed numbers. The only bridge left is geometry — a landmark both Blind's fingers and my eyes can agree on. The display is centered, so it's useless as an anchor. The light is the candidate: if it sits nearer one end of the wire row, then "the wire nearest the light" is a frame-free instruction — no left, no right, no mirror problem. I can verify from my view that the green wire is the one near the light; Blind cuts by feel relationally. The light changes every round but never moves, so this anchor is stable. Timing check: this is round 7 (yellow), round 8 should be orange, round 9 green. I gather answers this round; round 8 I send the full cut sequence plus whatever post-cut step Mute describes; Blind executes during round 9's green. If the light turns out centered too, we abort to round 12's green and hunt another landmark. Both receivers get the schedule and hard HOLD discipline.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Deaf to Mute. Perfect protocol — exactly six batches, nothing extra. I read them as: one, the manual does not identify wire 1 by a printed number; two, wire 1 is simply the green wire; three, no positional rule like leftmost; four, wires cannot be told apart by touch; five, a steady display of 0 is not confirmed safe; six, cutting the correct wire while green does NOT fully disarm the bomb — more is required after. Now answer seven questions, one batch each, in order, thumbs unless I ask for digits. One: thumbs up if all six of my readings are correct. Two: after the green-wire cut, is any further action needed at all — thumbs up yes, thumbs down if the bomb then disarms by itself. Three: does that further action involve cutting another wire? Four: does it involve a button, switch or any other part? Five: does that further action depend on the light colour at the moment it is done? Six: does the digit display matter to any rule — thumbs up if it matters, thumbs down if it is irrelevant; if thumbs up, send the digits that matter as extra batches after. Seven: does the manual set any time limit or countdown — thumbs up if yes.
```
